question: What is a gene?
options: The complete set of DNA in an organism
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A type of chromosome found in gametes
A mutation in the DNA sequence
correct: A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein

question: What does homozygous mean?
options: Having two different alleles for a gene
Having one dominant and one recessive allele
Having two identical alleles for a gene
Having no alleles for a gene
correct: Having two identical alleles for a gene

question: A dominant allele is represented by B and recessive by b. Which genotype would show the recessive phenotype?
options: BB
Bb
bB
bb

question: What type of cell division produces gametes?
options: Mitosis
Binary fission
Meiosis
Budding

question: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two carrier parents (Ff × Ff) have a child. What is the probability the child has cystic fibrosis?
Which statement about polydactyly is correct?
options: It is caused by a recessive allele and causes thick mucus in the lungs
It is caused by a dominant allele and results in extra fingers or toes
It is caused by a recessive allele and results in extra fingers or toes
It is caused by a dominant allele and causes thick mucus in the lungs
correct: It is caused by a dominant allele and results in extra fingers or toes

question: What sex chromosomes does a human male have?
options: XX
XY
YY
X only

question: Which of the following is an example of continuous variation?
options: Blood group
Tongue rolling
Height
Attached or free earlobes

question: What is natural selection?
options: Humans selecting organisms with desirable traits to breed
The process by which better adapted individuals survive and pass on their genes
A random change in the DNA sequence
The formation of new species through isolation
correct: The process by which better adapted individuals survive and pass on their genes

question: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
options: Gregor Mendel
Louis Pasteur
Charles Darwin
Alexander Fleming

question: What is selective breeding?
options: Inserting a gene from one organism into another
Humans choosing organisms with desired traits and breeding them together
The natural process of evolution over millions of years
A type of mutation that improves an organism's characteristics
correct: Humans choosing organisms with desired traits and breeding them together

question: How is human insulin now produced commercially?
options: By extracting it from pigs and cows
By inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria
By synthesising it entirely from chemicals
By selective breeding of insulin-producing animals
correct: By inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria

question: What do fossils provide evidence for?
options: How organisms are classified into kingdoms
How species have changed over millions of years
The exact DNA sequence of extinct organisms
How genetic engineering works
correct: How species have changed over millions of years

question: What is a mutation?
options: The passing of alleles from parent to offspring
A random change in the DNA sequence
The fusion of two gametes at fertilisation
The separation of chromosomes during meiosis
correct: A random change in the DNA sequence

question: What does the binomial nomenclature system give each organism?
options: A common name in English
A two-part Latin name consisting of genus and species
A number based on its position in the food chain
A classification into one of five kingdoms
correct: A two-part Latin name consisting of genus and species

question: The complete set of genetic information of an organism is called its __________.
Different versions of the same gene are called __________.
The observable characteristics of an organism are called its __________.
The alleles an organism carries for a gene is called its __________.
Cell division that produces four genetically different haploid cells is called __________.
Cystic fibrosis is caused by a __________ allele.
A random change in the DNA sequence is called a __________.
The preserved remains of ancient organisms found in rock are called __________.
The process of modifying an organism's genome by inserting a gene from another organism is called __________ engineering.
The change in inherited characteristics of a population over many generations is called __________.
Match each genetic term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: Always expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present
Only expressed when two copies are present
Having two identical alleles for a gene
Having two different alleles for a gene

question: Match each inherited disorder to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Caused by a recessive allele — thick mucus in lungs and digestive system
Caused by a dominant allele — extra fingers or toes

question: Match each type of variation to its correct example.

pairs.definition: Height — shows a range of values with no distinct categories
Blood group — falls into distinct categories
Caused by mutations or sexual reproduction
A scar or a suntan — caused by the environment not genes

question: Match each piece of evidence to how it supports evolution.

pairs.definition: Show how species have changed over millions of years
Shows natural selection happening in bacteria in real time
Similar DNA sequences show common ancestry between species

question: Match each technique to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Humans breed organisms with desired traits over many generations
A gene is inserted from one organism into another to give a desired characteristic
Producing genetically identical copies of an organism

question: State what is meant by the term genome.
mark_scheme: The complete set of genetic information / DNA of an organism (1).

question: State the difference between genotype and phenotype.
mark_scheme: Genotype is the alleles an organism carries (1); phenotype is the observable characteristics resulting from the genotype (1) — accept either for 1 mark.

question: State the sex chromosomes found in a human female.
Name the scientist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection.
mark_scheme: Charles Darwin (1).

question: Explain why meiosis is important for sexual reproduction.
mark_scheme: Meiosis produces haploid gametes (1); containing half the normal number of chromosomes (1); so when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the full chromosome number is restored (1); produces genetic variation in offspring (1) — any two.

question: Explain how a mutation can lead to a new phenotype.
mark_scheme: A mutation is a random change in the DNA sequence (1); changes the sequence of bases (1); may alter the protein produced (1); this can result in a new or altered characteristic (1) — any two.

question: Describe how selective breeding is carried out.
mark_scheme: Identify individuals with the desired characteristic (1); breed these individuals together (1); select offspring with the desired characteristic (1); repeat over many generations (1) — any two.

question: Explain how antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an example of natural selection.
mark_scheme: Random mutation produces some resistant bacteria (1); antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria (1); resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (1); resistance genes passed to offspring (1) — any two.

question: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis (Ff). Explain the possible outcomes for their children.
mark_scheme: FF — unaffected and not a carrier (1); Ff — carrier but unaffected (1); ff — has cystic fibrosis (1); 25% chance of having the condition (1) — any two.

question: Explain the process of natural selection using an example.
mark_scheme: Variation exists within a population (1); some individuals have characteristics better suited to the environment (1); these individuals are more likely to survive and reproduce (1); they pass advantageous alleles to offspring (1); over many generations the advantageous characteristic becomes more common (1) — any three.

question: Describe how genetic engineering is used to produce human insulin.
mark_scheme: The gene for human insulin is identified and cut out (1); using enzymes (1); the gene is inserted into a bacterial plasmid (1); the bacteria reproduce and produce human insulin (1); insulin is harvested and purified (1) — any three.

question: Explain how sex is determined in humans.
mark_scheme: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (1); one pair are sex chromosomes (1); females are XX, males are XY (1); sperm carry either X or Y chromosome (1); eggs always carry X chromosome (1); if Y sperm fertilises egg — male; if X sperm — female (1) — any three.

question: Explain how Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection works, and why it was not immediately accepted.
mark_scheme: Variation exists in a population (1); individuals better adapted survive and reproduce (1); advantageous alleles passed to offspring (1); over many generations species change (1). Not accepted because: lack of fossil evidence at the time (1); conflicted with religious beliefs (1); mechanism of inheritance not understood (1) — any four.

question: Tall plants (T) are dominant over dwarf plants (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. Use a Punnett square to explain the expected ratio of tall to dwarf plants in the offspring.
mark_scheme: Both parents are Tt (1); Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt (1); 3 tall : 1 dwarf ratio (1); TT and Tt show tall phenotype (1); only tt shows dwarf phenotype (1) — any four.

question: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of selective breeding.
mark_scheme: Advantages: produces organisms with desired characteristics (1); can increase food production / disease resistance (1); has been practised successfully for thousands of years (1). Disadvantages: reduces genetic variation — inbreeding (1); may make populations vulnerable to new diseases (1); can cause health problems in animals e.g. hip problems in dogs (1) — any four.

question: Explain what fossils are and describe three types of evidence they provide for evolution.
mark_scheme: Fossils are preserved remains of ancient organisms (1); found in rock layers (1); show that organisms have changed over time (1); show common ancestors between species (1); gaps in fossil record show extinction events (1); older fossils in deeper rock layers (1) — any four.

question: Explain how cystic fibrosis is inherited. In your answer, use a genetic cross to show the possible outcomes when two carrier parents have children.
mark_scheme: Cystic fibrosis caused by recessive allele (1); carriers are heterozygous Ff (1); Punnett square: FF, Ff, Ff, ff (1); 25% chance of having cystic fibrosis (ff) (1); 50% chance of being a carrier (Ff) (1); 25% chance of being unaffected non-carrier (FF) (1) — any five.

question: Evaluate the use of genetic engineering in medicine and agriculture. Include both advantages and disadvantages in your answer.
mark_scheme: Advantages: produces human insulin for diabetics (1); can produce disease-resistant crops (1); faster than selective breeding (1); can introduce entirely new characteristics (1). Disadvantages: ethical concerns about 'playing God' (1); GM crops may affect ecosystems (1); long-term effects unknown (1); patented seeds may be expensive for farmers (1); risk of genes spreading to wild plants (1) — any six.

question: Explain how speciation occurs when populations become geographically isolated. Include the roles of variation, natural selection and mutation in your answer.
mark_scheme: A population becomes geographically isolated (1); no interbreeding between groups (1); variation exists within each group (1); different environmental pressures cause different natural selection (1); mutations occur randomly in each group (1); different alleles become more common in each group (1); over time the groups become so different they can no longer interbreed (1); a new species has formed (1) — any six.

question: Explain how DNA stores genetic information and how this information is used to make proteins.
mark_scheme: DNA is made of two strands in a double helix (1); bases pair up — A with T, C with G (1); a gene is a sequence of bases that codes for a protein (1); the sequence of bases determines the sequence of amino acids (1); different sequences of amino acids fold into different proteins with different functions (1) — any four.

question: Explain what is meant by codominance and give an example from human genetics.
mark_scheme: Codominance is where both alleles are expressed in the phenotype (1); neither allele is dominant over the other (1); both contribute to the phenotype (1); example: blood group AB — both A and B alleles expressed (1); individual has both A and B antigens on red blood cells (1) — any four.

question: Describe the differences between continuous and discontinuous variation. Give one example of each and state the causes.
mark_scheme: Continuous variation shows a range of values with no distinct categories (1); e.g. height, mass, foot size (1); caused by both genes and environment (1); discontinuous variation falls into distinct categories (1); e.g. blood group, sex, tongue rolling (1); usually controlled by one or a few genes (1) — any four.

question: Explain why a person can carry the allele for cystic fibrosis without showing any symptoms of the disease.
mark_scheme: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (1); a carrier has one recessive allele and one dominant allele (heterozygous) (1); the dominant allele masks the recessive allele (1); the dominant allele results in normal mucus production (1); only individuals with two recessive alleles (homozygous) develop cystic fibrosis (1) — any four.

question: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using genetic engineering to produce GM crops.
mark_scheme: Advantages: can produce crops resistant to pests reducing pesticide use (1); crops can be made drought-resistant improving yields (1); can improve nutritional content e.g. golden rice (1). Disadvantages: potential environmental impact — gene may spread to wild plants (1); reduced biodiversity (1); unknown long-term effects on human health (1); ethical concerns (1) — any four.

question: Explain how the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria provides evidence for natural selection.
mark_scheme: Bacteria show random variation / mutations (1); some bacteria have mutations that make them resistant to antibiotics (1); when antibiotics are given, non-resistant bacteria are killed (1); resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (1); resistance genes are passed to offspring (1); over time, resistant bacteria become more common in the population (1) — any four.

question: Explain the importance of studying the human genome for medicine and understanding human evolution.
mark_scheme: Genome is the complete set of DNA / all genes of an organism (1); studying it can identify genes linked to inherited diseases (1); allows genetic screening and diagnosis (1); can help develop gene therapy (1); comparing genomes shows evolutionary relationships between species (1); helps trace human migration and ancestry (1) — any four.

question: Describe the process of meiosis and explain why it is important for genetic variation.
mark_scheme: Meiosis is a type of cell division (1); produces four daughter cells (1); daughter cells are haploid — containing half the chromosome number (1); each cell is genetically different (1); chromosomes cross over and exchange segments during meiosis (1); this increases genetic variation (1) — any four.

question: Explain how geographical isolation can lead to the formation of a new species.
mark_scheme: A population becomes separated by a physical barrier (1); two groups can no longer interbreed (1); each group is subject to different environmental pressures (1); natural selection favours different characteristics in each group (1); over many generations, genetic differences accumulate (1); the two groups eventually become so different they cannot interbreed — a new species forms (1) — any four.

question: Compare selective breeding and genetic engineering as methods of improving the characteristics of organisms.
mark_scheme: Selective breeding: selects individuals with desired traits and breeds them (1); takes many generations (1); only works with existing variation within/between species (1). Genetic engineering: directly inserts a gene from another organism (1); faster — can achieve change in one generation (1); can introduce entirely new characteristics not present in the species (1); but raises greater ethical concerns (1) — any four.

question: Explain how evidence from DNA analysis and the fossil record together support the theory of evolution.
mark_scheme: Fossils show organisms have changed over time (1); older fossils found in deeper rock layers (1); show gradual changes in structure over millions of years (1); DNA analysis compares gene sequences between species (1); similar DNA suggests common ancestor (1); more similar DNA = more closely related (1) — any four.

question: Explain the structure of DNA, including the names of the bases and how they pair together.
mark_scheme: DNA is a double helix (1); made of two strands wound around each other (1); each strand is made of nucleotides (1); each nucleotide contains a sugar, phosphate and a base (1); four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine, guanine (1); complementary base pairing: A pairs with T, C pairs with G (1) — any five.

question: Evaluate the use of embryo screening and genetic testing to detect inherited disorders such as cystic fibrosis.
mark_scheme: Genetic testing can identify if parents are carriers (1); embryo screening during IVF tests embryos for the faulty allele (1); only unaffected embryos are implanted (1); reduces number of children born with cystic fibrosis (1); ethical concerns — unused embryos are destroyed (1); some argue this is morally wrong (1); can cause anxiety for parents (1) — any five.

question: Explain how mutations can affect the phenotype of an organism, and why most mutations have no effect.
mark_scheme: A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence (1); changes the codon / triplet code (1); may result in a different amino acid being added to the protein (1); this can change the shape of the protein and its function (1); most mutations occur in non-coding regions of DNA and have no effect (1); some mutations are silent — code for the same amino acid (1); rarely, a mutation may give a beneficial characteristic (1) — any five.

question: Describe the process of genetic engineering, including the role of enzymes and plasmids.
mark_scheme: The desired gene is identified in the donor organism's DNA (1); restriction enzymes cut the gene out (1); the same restriction enzyme cuts open a bacterial plasmid (1); the gene is inserted into the plasmid using ligase enzyme (1); the recombinant plasmid is inserted into a bacterium (1); the bacterium reproduces producing many copies (1); bacteria transcribe the gene producing the desired protein (1) — any five.

question: A woman is a carrier of the allele for red-green colour blindness, which is X-linked and recessive. Her partner has normal vision. Explain the possible outcomes for their children.
mark_scheme: Colour blindness is X-linked — on the X chromosome (1); mother is X^B X^b — carrier (1); father is X^B Y — normal vision (1); daughters: X^B X^B (unaffected) or X^B X^b (carrier) — 50% probability each (1); sons: X^B Y (normal) or X^b Y (colour blind) — 50% probability each (1); daughters cannot be colour blind as they would need two recessive alleles (1) — any five.

question: Evaluate the evidence for and against Lamarck's and Darwin's theories of evolution.
mark_scheme: Lamarck: organisms develop characteristics during their lifetime that are passed on (1); e.g. giraffes stretched necks and passed on longer necks (1); disproved — acquired characteristics are not inherited (1); Darwin: variation exists in populations (1); best adapted individuals survive and reproduce — natural selection (1); supported by fossil record, DNA evidence and observed examples like antibiotic resistance (1); Darwin's theory is now well supported by genetics (1) — any five.

question: Explain how the discovery of the structure of DNA by Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins was a significant milestone in biology.
mark_scheme: The double helix structure was described in 1953 (1); Watson and Crick built on X-ray crystallography images from Rosalind Franklin (1); the structure explained how DNA could be copied — complementary base pairing (1); explained how genetic information is stored as a base sequence (1); led to understanding of how genes code for proteins (1); opened the way for genetic engineering and medicine (1) — any five.

question: Describe polydactyly and explain why it is found in every generation of an affected family.
mark_scheme: Polydactyly is the presence of extra fingers or toes (1); caused by a dominant allele (1); only one copy of the allele is needed to show the condition (1); an affected parent has at least one dominant allele (1); 50% of children will inherit the allele and be affected (1); condition cannot skip a generation as any individual with the allele shows it (1) — any five.

question: Explain the role of sexual reproduction in producing genetic variation, and explain why genetic variation is important for the survival of a species.
mark_scheme: Sexual reproduction involves meiosis producing genetically different gametes (1); random fertilisation produces unique combinations of alleles (1); offspring are genetically different from each other and from parents (1); genetic variation means individuals within a population differ (1); if the environment changes some individuals may be better adapted (1); better adapted individuals survive and reproduce — natural selection (1); without variation all individuals could be wiped out by a new disease (1) — any five.

question: Describe how selective breeding has been used to improve livestock, and discuss the problems that can arise from this process.
mark_scheme: Farmers identify animals with desired traits e.g. high milk yield or muscle mass (1); these animals are bred together (1); offspring with the best traits are selected and bred again (1); repeated over many generations (1); can produce animals with highly desirable characteristics (1); but reduces genetic diversity — inbreeding (1); can lead to health problems in animals e.g. hip dysplasia in dogs (1) — any five.

question: Explain what is meant by incomplete dominance and how it differs from the inheritance pattern seen in simple dominant/recessive crosses.
mark_scheme: In incomplete dominance, neither allele is fully dominant (1); the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype (1); e.g. red × white flowers give pink offspring (1); in simple dominance, one allele fully masks the other (1); heterozygous individuals show the same phenotype as homozygous dominant (1); in incomplete dominance three distinct phenotypes are possible (1) — any five.

question: Explain how the genome can be used to understand inherited disease, trace human evolution and develop new medicines.
mark_scheme: The genome is the complete DNA sequence of an organism (1); comparing genomes allows scientists to identify genes linked to disease (1); genetic screening can identify people at risk of inherited conditions (1); gene therapy aims to correct faulty genes (1); comparing human genomes with other species shows evolutionary relationships (1); similar gene sequences indicate common ancestry (1); new drugs can be designed to target specific proteins coded for by certain genes (1); personalised medicine can be tailored to an individual's genome (1) — any six.

question: Evaluate the benefits and ethical concerns of using genetic screening to test for inherited conditions before and after birth.
mark_scheme: Pre-birth screening: can detect conditions such as Down's syndrome or cystic fibrosis (1); allows parents to make informed decisions (1); may lead to termination of pregnancy — ethical concern (1); some argue embryos / foetuses have a right to life (1); post-birth screening: newborn blood spot tests identify treatable conditions early (1); early treatment can prevent complications (1); may cause anxiety if a carrier is identified (1); insurance and employment discrimination concerns (1); benefit of knowledge must be balanced against psychological impact (1) — any six.

question: Explain the role of chromosomes and alleles in inheritance, and use a genetic cross to show how a recessive condition such as cystic fibrosis can be inherited.
mark_scheme: Chromosomes carry genes made of DNA (1); each gene can have different versions called alleles (1); one allele inherited from each parent (1); cystic fibrosis caused by recessive allele (f) (1); carriers are Ff — heterozygous (1); cross Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff (1); 25% chance of ff — cystic fibrosis (1); 50% chance of Ff — carrier (1) — any six.

question: Explain how Darwin developed his theory of evolution by natural selection. Include the evidence he gathered and the reasons why his ideas were controversial.
mark_scheme: Darwin observed variation in populations during his voyage on the Beagle (1); noted that organisms produce more offspring than can survive (1); individuals with advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive (1); these individuals pass on their traits to offspring (1); over many generations, advantageous traits become more common (1); controversial because it challenged religious beliefs about creation (1); lacked a mechanism to explain inheritance (genetics not yet understood) (1); insufficient fossil evidence at the time (1) — any six.

question: Evaluate the use of genetic engineering compared to selective breeding for improving crops. In your answer, consider the effectiveness, speed, risks and ethical issues of each method.
mark_scheme: Selective breeding: well-established and widely accepted (1); takes many generations — slow (1); limited to traits within the species or closely related species (1). Genetic engineering: can introduce traits from any organism including different species (1); results achieved in one generation — much faster (1); can produce crops with new traits e.g. herbicide resistance, improved nutrition (1). Risks of GM crops: genes may spread to wild plants (1); reduced biodiversity (1); unknown health effects (1); ethical concerns about modifying organisms (1) — any six.

question: Explain how scientists classify organisms into groups, and describe how advances in DNA technology have changed the way classification is done.
mark_scheme: Classification organises organisms into groups based on shared characteristics (1); traditional classification used observable features: body structure, reproduction, nutrition (1); organisms grouped into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species (1); species given a two-part Latin name — binomial nomenclature (1); DNA technology allows comparison of gene sequences between organisms (1); organisms with more similar DNA sequences are more closely related (1); DNA analysis has led to reclassification of some organisms (1); e.g. three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) replacing the five-kingdom system (1) — any six.

question: Explain how sex is determined in humans. Include a genetic cross showing the possible sex of children and explain why the probability of having a boy or girl is approximately 50:50.
mark_scheme: Sex is determined by sex chromosomes (1); females have two X chromosomes (XX) (1); males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY) (1); eggs always contain an X chromosome (1); sperm carry either an X or a Y chromosome (1); cross XX × XY gives XX (female) or XY (male) (1); equal numbers of X-carrying and Y-carrying sperm produced (1); each sperm has equal chance of fertilising the egg so 50:50 ratio (1) — any six.

question: Evaluate the importance of genetic variation in the survival of species, using examples to illustrate your answer.
mark_scheme: Genetic variation is the differences in alleles between individuals in a population (1); arises through mutation and sexual reproduction (1); variation means some individuals may be better adapted if the environment changes (1); e.g. if a new disease appears, some individuals may have resistance (1); these individuals survive and reproduce passing on the advantageous alleles (1); species with low genetic variation are more vulnerable to extinction (1); e.g. cheetahs have very low genetic diversity making them susceptible to disease (1); conservation programmes aim to maintain genetic diversity (1) — any six.
